rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall retention window without risking truncation. This gives a good first read on whether peaks are bunched early, spread through the gradient, or still eluting during the final hold.

The first run shows all peaks eluting within a narrow effective solvent window, so trim the gradient to focus on that region and keep all peaks inside the gradient. A narrower window at the same tG makes the gradient shallower and should improve the close mid-run pairs while likely reducing total run time.

The narrowed window was too slow, but injection 1 suggests we already have full resolution, so now test a steeper gradient to cut analysis time while checking whether the critical 6/7 pair remains comfortably resolved. This slope comparison against the 20 min broad gradient will also reveal how sensitive the close pairs are to gradient steepness.

The 10 min gradient is too steep for the 5-7 cluster, while 20 min fully resolves it but costs time, so test an intermediate slope to find the shortest broad-window method that restores acceptable resolution. This directly brackets the optimum between injections 1 and 3.

Resolution of the critical 6/7 pair improves strongly with longer tG, and 14 min is close but not quite there, so try 16 min to see if it clears the threshold while still keeping the run short. This should be near the optimum if selectivity is dominated by slope rather than temperature.

Since 14 min is faster but just misses on the 6/7 pair, test a small temperature decrease to shift selectivity without sacrificing time. If that pair is temperature-sensitive, this could beat the current best by restoring resolution while keeping the short run.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity, so try the opposite direction at the same 14 min slope to see whether the critical cluster opens up at higher temperature. A favorable temperature shift here could surpass the current best by keeping the zero time penalty of the 14 min method.

Temperature clearly changes which pair is limiting, so probe a larger selectivity shift at a faster gradient where a temperature win would be most valuable. If 25 C separates the critical cluster better than 40 C, this could achieve full resolution with a shorter run than the current 16 min method.

Temperature changes have been unfavorable, and the main tradeoff is now simply slope versus time around the broad-window method. Test 18 min to see whether it gives full resolution like 20 min but with less time penalty than the current fully resolved 16 min run.

All compounds elute by about phi_e 0.57 in the broad runs, so lowering phi1 while keeping phi0 and tG fixed trims unused high-organic space and slightly shallows the gradient where the critical cluster sits. This may improve the 6/7 separation without adding enough time to lose the strong CRF of the 14 min method.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.85 improved the 14 min method to full resolution with only a small time cost, so step phi1 down once more to further shallow the gradient near the elution window. This may preserve full resolution while trimming the time penalty even closer to zero.

phi1 = 0.85 appears close to optimal, but we only bracketed it coarsely with 0.80 and 0.95; testing 0.90 checks whether a slightly steeper trimmed window reduces run time enough while keeping full resolution. This should define the local optimum in phi1 around the current best method.

The 14 min, phi1 0.90 method is very strong, but the limiting pair is still only modestly resolved, so test whether the slightly shallower 12 min/0.85 combination preserves enough selectivity while cutting time further. This is a logical interpolation between the fast but too-steep 10 min broad run and the successful 14 min trimmed runs.

The best current point is 14 min, phi1 0.90 with no time penalty but only marginal 6/7 resolution, so test a small increase in tG at the same trimmed window to see if the resolution term reaches 1.000 while keeping the time penalty very small. This is the most direct local refinement around the current optimum.

The earliest peak is still well retained, so raising phi0 slightly trims unused low-organic time and may reduce runtime while keeping the same successful upper window. This tests whether the best 14 min, phi1 0.90 method can be made a bit faster without collapsing the critical 6/7 pair.

Raising phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved the method further, and the first peak is still not near dead time, so test one more step higher to see if we can trim additional unproductive early time. This checks whether the current best can be improved without sacrificing the still-acceptable critical-pair resolution.

The best method uses phi0 0.10, and lowering phi1 from 0.95 helped earlier, so combine those favorable changes to see whether a slightly narrower window improves the critical 6/7 pair enough to maximize the resolution term without adding a meaningful time penalty. This is the most promising local refinement around the current best.

We have already reached the maximum CRF, so use remaining budget only to map nearby robustness. Testing phi0 one step higher at the winning phi1 checks whether the optimum is broad or if early compression starts to erode the first peaks or the critical mid-cluster.

We already have multiple maximum-CRF methods, so continue defining the robust plateau by increasing phi0 another step at the winning phi1 and tG. This tests how far the low-end trimming can go before the first peaks approach the unretained region or mid-cluster resolution degrades.

Since phi0 0.10 works well, test whether reducing phi1 at that same lower-end setting still stays on the CRF plateau. This maps the lower bound of the successful gradient window around the already optimal region.

We now know phi1 0.80 is too low at phi0 0.10, but phi0 0.15 gives a shorter window and has already matched the maximum at phi1 0.85. Testing phi0 0.15 with phi1 0.80 checks whether the successful plateau extends diagonally toward a tighter, faster solvent window.

We have maxed out CRF at 14 min, so with the remaining budget test whether the winning solvent window still works at a shorter gradient. This directly probes the lower tG boundary of the optimum plateau around the best method.

The winning window still loses some critical-pair resolution at 12 min, so test whether the slightly higher phi0 variant that also reached CRF 1.000 at 14 min behaves better at the shorter gradient. This helps define whether phi0 0.10 or 0.15 is the more robust edge of the optimum plateau.

With the optimum plateau established at 14 min, use a remaining shot to bracket it on the slower side for robustness at the exact winning solvent window. This confirms whether 14 min is truly the local optimum in tG for phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85.

Use the final run to complete the local robustness map around the two winning methods by testing the slower-side tG at the second max-CRF composition. This confirms whether both CRF=1.000 optima share the same narrow tG dependence.
